security_audit.summary: Most alerts are false positives caused by Markdown inline code and prose references to shells. Confirmed risks include environment-controlled command selection and retrying an Orca command with elevated permissions. The stub also delegates instructions to an unaudited guide, which weakens marketplace review coverage.

remediation.issue: The ORCA_CLI_COMMAND value is used as an executable without validation.
remediation.suggestion: Require an approved executable path and reject arguments, shell operators, or unexpected command names.

remediation.issue: The audited stub delegates behavior to guide content that is absent from the package.
remediation.suggestion: Bundle the complete guide or cryptographically verify and separately audit every guide version before use.

remediation.issue: The guide tells agents to retry a failed command with elevated permissions.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user approval and document the exact command, permission scope, and reason before escalation.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 17 uses Markdown backticks around command names. It contains no Ruby or shell backtick execution.
Although the backticks are Markdown, line 24 directs the agent to execute an environment-controlled value. A modified environment can select an unintended command.
Line 26 names a fixed Orca development executable in Markdown. It does not contain shell substitution or dynamic execution syntax.
Line 27 names the fixed orca-ide command and warns about choosing the wrong executable. The backticks are documentation formatting.
Line 28 is prose containing an inline command name. No executable backtick construct is present.
Line 29 documents a system path to explain a command-name collision. It does not execute that path.
Line 30 selects a fixed installed Orca executable for the skill's stated purpose. The finding specifically mistakes Markdown backticks for shell execution.
Line 32 defines ORCA as a documentation placeholder. It contains no executable shell syntax.
Line 33 explicitly says not to run the placeholder literally. Its backticks only format the placeholder name.
Line 41 opens a fenced text block. It is Markdown structure, not Ruby or shell execution.
Line 43 closes a fenced text block. It is Markdown structure, not executable syntax.
Line 45 documents output and help flags with inline Markdown. It contains no shell substitution.
Line 46 directs the agent to run the selected executable. If selection came from ORCA_CLI_COMMAND, this can invoke an environment-controlled command.
Line 47 quotes an error identifier for troubleshooting. It does not execute a command.
Line 48 instructs the agent to rerun a command with elevated permissions without requiring user approval or limiting the permission scope.
Line 49 uses inline Markdown for a subcommand and flag while describing read-only troubleshooting. No backtick execution occurs.
Line 34 states that placeholder substitution works in PowerShell. It neither invokes PowerShell nor supplies a PowerShell command.
Line 34 mentions cmd.exe as a compatible shell. It does not invoke cmd.exe or provide executable Windows syntax.
Line 7 describes simulator evidence as a supported use case. It performs no host, network, identity, or system reconnaissance.
Line 8 directs Android users to another skill and notes build prerequisites. It does not inspect the system.

content.value_statement: iOS testing often requires switching between agent tools, simulator controls, and evidence collection. This skill routes simulator interaction through Orca and loads guidance matched to the active CLI.
actual_capabilities: Resolves the Orca CLI for managed, development, Linux, and standard sessions.
Loads simulator guidance matched to the selected Orca executable.
Supports workflows for taps, gestures, typing, rotation, and hardware buttons.
Supports accessibility tree inspection and simulator evidence collection.
Provides recovery guidance when Orca is unavailable or access is denied.
limitations: Requires a booted Apple Simulator on macOS.
Requires the application to be built and installed before simulator control.
Does not support Android devices or Android emulators.
Depends on guide content supplied by the installed Orca version.

use_cases.title: Verify an iOS Change
use_cases.description: Drive the changed interface and collect simulator evidence for a review.

use_cases.title: Repeat Interface Checks
use_cases.description: Perform consistent taps, typing, gestures, and rotation during exploratory testing.

use_cases.title: Inspect Accessible Interfaces
use_cases.description: Review the simulator accessibility tree while investigating labels, controls, and navigation.

prompt_templates.title: Open and Inspect
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Orca to inspect the booted iOS Simulator. Report the visible screen and available accessibility elements before taking action.

prompt_templates.title: Complete a Basic Flow
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Orca to open [app], tap [control], enter [text], and report the final visible state.

prompt_templates.title: Verify a UI Change
prompt_templates.prompt: Test [feature] in the booted simulator. Exercise [steps], inspect accessibility labels, and collect evidence for the expected result.

prompt_templates.title: Investigate a Stateful Failure
prompt_templates.prompt: Reproduce [failure] through Orca across [orientations or states]. Record each action, observed result, accessibility evidence, and the earliest divergence.

output_examples.input: Inspect the current simulator screen and identify the primary action.
output_examples.output: The simulator shows the sign-in screen. The primary accessible action is Sign In, below the email and password fields.

output_examples.input: Rotate the simulator and verify the checkout screen.
output_examples.output: The checkout screen remained visible in landscape orientation. The order summary and Place Order control were accessible without overlap.

output_examples.input: Reproduce the failed profile update and collect evidence.
output: Opened Profile and changed the display name.
Tapped Save and observed an error banner.
The original name remained after reopening the screen.

best_practices: Resolve the Orca executable once and use the same executable throughout the session.
Inspect the current screen and accessibility tree before issuing interactions.
Record expected and observed states when collecting simulator evidence.
anti_patterns: Do not use this skill for Android devices or emulators.
Do not guess unsupported Orca commands when help output is available.
Do not change executables after a failure because another build may target different session state.

faq.question: What platform does this skill support?
faq.answer: It supports a booted Apple iOS Simulator on macOS through Orca.

faq.question: Can it build and install my application?
faq.answer: No. Build and install the application with Xcode tooling or simctl before using this skill.

faq.question: Does it support Android emulators?
faq.answer: No. Use the separate Android emulator skill for Android devices and emulators.

faq.question: What interactions can it guide?
faq.answer: It covers taps, gestures, typing, hardware buttons, rotation, accessibility inspection, and evidence collection.

faq.question: Why does it load another guide?
faq.answer: It requests guidance matched to the active Orca executable and session version.

faq.question: What should happen when the selected executable fails?
faq.answer: Report the exact error and stop. Do not switch to another Orca executable.
